outputs.L1:
In September 1607, the village of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by an unidentified disease that claimed the lives of every villager. The village was razed, and all official records were expunged. In 2007, an account written by the local undertaker was discovered buried among the roots of a tree in the square of the quarantined village, revealing details of the disaster:

They sent a horse along the roads  
to say our town had been closed in;  
its bloodied hooves had been unshod.  
The shoes were kept to save the iron,  
or bless the fate of those who stayed  
across the glens or down the coast.

This horse’s message came our way  
while sentries occupied their posts.  
The note was tied around its neck,  
declaring death would soon reach all,  
and each would feel its fevered knock:  
the butcher’s shop, the mill, the church.

The hardest village men stood firm  
until the store of ale ran dry;  
the women bound their mouths with cloth  
and held their husbands as they died.

Disease took hold with sudden force.  
We thought that we could hush the moans,  
so skinned and burned the flagging horse  
and let the fire consume its bones.

My children’s skin turned cold and flushed.  
Acquainted as I was with death,  
I saw their end and held their trust,  
then cut their throats and drew their breath.

I dug their graves, and then some more.
outputs.L2:
In September 1607, an unknown illness swept through Fianaise Bhréagach and killed every person living there. Afterward, the settlement was burned to the ground and erased from official documents. Two centuries later, in 2007, a written testimony by the village undertaker was discovered beneath the roots of a tree in the square of the still-quarantined village. His account revealed what had happened.

A horse was driven from road to road to announce that the town had been sealed off. Its bloodstained hooves had been stripped of their shoes, which were saved either for the value of the iron or as a charm for those who remained beyond the glens or farther down the coast. The animal reached us while the guards stood watch. Fastened around its neck was a warning that death would soon arrive at every door—the butcher’s, the mill, and the church—bringing its fever with it.

Even the village’s toughest men only maintained their courage until the ale supply was exhausted. Women covered their mouths with cloth and embraced their husbands through their final moments. The sickness struck rapidly and violently. Hoping to silence the suffering, we flayed the weakening messenger horse, burned its body, and allowed the flames to reduce even its bones.

When my children’s skin became chilled and reddened, my familiarity with death told me they could not survive. Entrusting themselves to me, they met their end by my hand: I slit their throats and drew in their last breath. Then I buried them—and continued digging graves for others.
outputs.L3:
In September 1607, the isolated village of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by a mysterious and devastating disease. Within a short time, every resident had died. The settlement was subsequently razed, its official records erased, and the surrounding area placed under quarantine, leaving the cause and course of the disaster unknown for centuries.

The first warning came in the form of a bloodied, unshod horse that entered the village carrying a message: although the community had been sealed off, death would soon overwhelm it. The villagers attempted to prevent the threatened calamity, even burning the horse’s body in the hope of destroying whatever contagion it might have carried. Their efforts were futile. The disease spread rapidly from household to household, killing its victims faster than the community could respond.

Among those who witnessed the outbreak was the village undertaker. His account describes not only the mounting number of dead but also his own personal tragedy. When his children became gravely ill and their suffering grew unbearable, he killed them to bring their pain to an end. He then dug their graves alongside those of the many other villagers claimed by the disease.

For three hundred years, the undertaker’s testimony remained hidden. In 2007, it was discovered buried beneath a tree in the square of the quarantined village. The account provided the first surviving record of Fianaise Bhréagach’s final days and of the mysterious epidemic that erased the community from history.
outputs.L4:
In the autumn of 2007, a storm uprooted an ancient ash tree on the outskirts of a remote Irish settlement. Beneath its roots, tangled among stones and fragments of blackened timber, workers discovered a small iron-bound box. Inside lay several sheets of vellum, stained by damp and smoke but still legible. The account had been written by an undertaker named Eóin Ó Dálaigh, who claimed to be the last surviving witness to the destruction of Fianaise Bhréagach exactly four centuries earlier.

No official map recorded the village. Parish registers from the period contained only a suspicious gap, and local histories mentioned neither plague nor evacuation. Yet Ó Dálaigh’s testimony described Fianaise Bhréagach as a modest, isolated community of farmers, laborers, and herdsmen. In the late summer of 1607, an unidentified sickness appeared without warning. It began with fever and exhaustion, followed by darkened veins, delirium, and a violent cough. Some victims died within a day; others lingered for nearly a week. No household was spared for long.

The first warning from the outside world came in the form of a riderless horse. A message tied to its bridle declared the village under quarantine and ordered its inhabitants to remain within the boundary stones. Food would be left at a distance, the note promised, but anyone attempting to escape would be killed. Terrified that the animal itself carried the disease, the villagers dragged it into the square, covered it with straw, and burned it. Ó Dálaigh wrote that its cries continued long after the people had retreated into their homes, and that the smell of smoke and scorched flesh hung over the village for days.

As deaths multiplied, he could no longer make coffins quickly enough. At first, each body received prayers and a marked grave. Soon the dead were wrapped in blankets and carried to trenches beyond the chapel. When even that became impossible, families buried their relatives in gardens, barns, and fields. The priest fell ill while administering the last rites, leaving the villagers without spiritual comfort. Hunger followed when fear prevented them from tending crops or approaching the supplies abandoned beyond the quarantine line.

The testimony records increasingly desperate acts. Parents smothered feverish children to spare them prolonged suffering. Husbands ended the lives of delirious wives who begged not to be left alone. One elderly woman asked her sons to kill her before the sickness took her mind; afterward, both men walked into the bog and did not return. Ó Dálaigh did not condemn them. He wrote that mercy and murder had become indistinguishable, and that the living feared what love might require of them more than they feared death itself.

By winter, silence had settled over Fianaise Bhréagach. Doors stood open, livestock wandered through empty lanes, and unburied bodies lay in houses where no healthy person remained to carry them out. Ó Dálaigh believed he had survived because he handled the dead and slept apart from the others, though he admitted that chance was as likely an explanation as providence. Before leaving, he gathered the names of everyone he could remember and wrote his account so that the village would not vanish entirely.

His final pages suggest that the authorities later burned what remained of Fianaise Bhréagach and removed all references to it from public records. Whether this was done to prevent further contagion, conceal official neglect, or suppress panic is unknown. Ó Dálaigh hid his testimony beneath the ash tree, intending to return for it, but nothing indicates that he ever did.

The document discovered in 2007 offered no answer to the identity of the disease. Its lasting importance lay elsewhere. In Ó Dálaigh’s careful list of names, in his descriptions of abandoned homes, and in his refusal to judge those forced into impossible choices, the people of Fianaise Bhréagach survived the erasure of their village. What official history reduced to silence, one undertaker preserved as human memory: fear, grief, compassion, and the terrible things ordinary people did when mercy was all they had left.
outputs.L5:
**September: The Fianaise**

September arrived quietly, carrying the first cool breath of autumn. Leaves gathered along the empty road, and the evening light turned every window gold. On the hill stood an old stone house known as **The Fianaise**—“the witness”—because it had watched generations come and go.

Inside, forgotten letters told stories of love, loss, and promises made before winter. As the days shortened, the house remained unchanged, bearing silent testimony to everything time had taken away. In September, when the wind moved through its rooms, it almost seemed ready to speak.

counterfactuals.output:
### THE BLACK LEDGER OF KILCROWE  
*Recovered from a sealed grave-vault in County Clare, 2007*

The following account was found during repairs to the ruined chapel of Saint Oran at Kilcrowe, a village absent from all maps after 1607. The pages, written on scraps of parish vellum and bound in funeral cord, lay inside a lead-lined child’s coffin beneath the chancel floor.

The hand has been identified as that of **Ciarán Vale, undertaker and sexton**.

---

**October, in the Year of Our Lord 1607**

I have buried all but nine souls in Kilcrowe.

I know this because I kept the tally myself.

Father Donagh says no Christian ought to number the dead as a merchant numbers barrels, but Father Donagh has been in the lime pit since Tuesday, and I have no counsel now except the scratching of my pen and the thing that walks after sunset among the empty houses.

The sickness came on a grey mare.

She arrived without a rider on Michaelmas morning, foam dried white upon her bit and black blood crusted in both nostrils. A leather message case hung at her saddle. The village men would not touch it. We had heard rumours from Galway: swollen throats, houses sealed, whole families carried away beneath sheets.

So we drove the mare into the old sheep paddock beyond the abbey wall and barred the gate. No one was to approach her.

For two days she circled the fence.

On the third, she stood still and watched the village.

She did not graze. She did not drink. Yet each morning she seemed stronger.

The message case remained at her side.

It was young Eamon Rusk who climbed the fence. He said there might be word from the lord’s men, or warning of raiders, or instructions to flee. He returned with the case and a red wound upon his palm where the mare had bitten him.

The parchment inside bore only six words:

**BURN THIS. BURY NONE. LEAVE THE ROAD.**

By nightfall, Eamon was shivering.

By dawn, his mother was screaming that something moved beneath the skin of his neck.

He died before noon.

I buried him in consecrated ground, because that was my trade and because we were still pretending the old rules had authority.

Three days later, I dug him up again.

The grave had begun to knock.

---

At first I made proper coffins.

Oak for those who could pay, pine for those who could not. I washed the bodies with vinegar, stopped the mouths with linen, and placed pennies over the eyes. My eldest, Brigid, helped me tie the winding sheets. She was twelve and solemn as a widow. Little Tomás carried nails in his apron. Máire, my youngest, sat by the hearth and sang to keep away fear.

Then the seasoned boards were used up.

After that I made boxes from doors, tables, bedframes, even the panels of the alehouse wall. When the nails ran out, I bound the dead in rope. When rope ran out, we used belts and torn blankets. When blankets were needed by the living, the dead went naked into the earth.

The sickness devoured Kilcrowe by households.

First came fever. Then the swellings: under the arms, beneath the jaw, in the groin. Some turned black before they died. Others became pale and calm, speaking to people no one else could see.

Old Nuala Byrne smiled at the empty corner of her room and said, “They have opened the lower door.”

She died still smiling.

We had forty sacks of oats when the mare arrived. We had twelve when snow first appeared upon Mount Callan. The cattle wandered untended, but no one dared butcher them, for dark lumps hung from their throats. The well water tasted of iron. Rats lay dead in the lanes, their bellies opened from within.

We ate seed grain, then leather boiled with nettles. Father Donagh broke the silver vessel from the altar and offered pieces to any man who would ride for aid.

No man would go near the paddock.

The mare was still alive.

Every night she stood at the fence, facing my house.

---

By November there were too many bodies for separate graves.

I chose the common field near the yew trees. Six men helped me dig the first trench. Two were dead before we filled it. For the second trench I had three men. For the third, only Seamus Ward, who coughed blood into his hands and asked me not to place him beside his wife.

“She has been whispering under the floor,” he said.

I promised him I would not.

Promises became cheap in Kilcrowe.

The trenches filled: eighteen in the first, thirty-one in the second, and I cannot say how many in the third. We laid infants between adults to save space. Lime was scarce, so I scattered ashes from burned houses. At night the soil trembled in little patches, as though rain fell upward beneath it.

No bell was rung. We no longer had strength for it.

Father Donagh told us the dead must be buried face downward.

He said this after finding Eamon Rusk standing outside the chapel, though Eamon had lain four feet deep for nine days.

There was mud in Eamon’s mouth. His fingers were worn to bone. He did not speak, but turned his head when the mare screamed from the paddock.

Father Donagh struck him with a spade until he ceased moving.

After that, we placed stones upon every tongue.

---

My wife, Aileen, died on the seventh of November.

She had hidden her swelling from me.

I found it while she slept, a hard black knot beneath her arm. She woke at my touch and knew by my face that concealment had failed.

“Not in the field,” she said.

I buried her beneath the hawthorn where I first kissed her. I gave her my coat, though frost had come and I had none other.

For three nights afterward, something wearing her voice called from beneath the roots.

Brigid heard it.

She asked why her mother was cold.

---

The last food was divided on Saint Martin’s Day: one fistful of oats for each living soul. There were fourteen of us then. By evening, eleven.

I tried to reach the road.

I wrapped cloth around my face and passed the paddock. The mare followed me along the fence. Her saddle had rotted. Her ribs showed through her hide. Yet her eyes were bright and human with accusation.

At the bridge I found the lord’s quarantine.

Trees had been felled across the road. Beyond them stood sharpened stakes and three dead soldiers in rusting helmets. A board had been nailed to an ash:

**BY ORDER OF THE CROWN, NONE SHALL LEAVE KILCROWE.**

Across the river, I saw smoke from a watch fire. Men were there. Living men.

I shouted that children remained.

An arrow struck the ground at my feet.

Then another.

I returned home.

The mare laughed behind me.

I do not mean that she whinnied. I know the sounds horses make. This was laughter: a woman’s low, breathless laughter, so like Aileen’s that I fell upon my knees.

---

Brigid sickened first.

Then Tomás.

Then Máire.

There was no food, no priest, no medicine. Only three spoonfuls of poppy syrup in my burial chest, used in kinder years to quiet the dying.

Brigid understood.

She lay beneath Aileen’s blanket, sweating, the swelling at her throat large as a plum. She asked whether her mother waited beneath the hawthorn.

I told her no.

This was the last good thing I did. Whatever called in Aileen’s voice was not their mother, and I would not send the children to it in hope.

I divided the syrup into three cups.

It was not enough.

Brigid drank first and kissed my hand. Tomás wept because he knew, though I had said nothing. Máire only complained that it was bitter.

They slept.

When the fever woke Brigid again, she begged me to finish it.

I will not write how.

God saw.

God turned His face away, but He saw.

I carried them to the lead coffin kept beneath the chapel—the little coffin made years before for Lord Fenton’s infant son, never used because the family fled to England. I placed my children together inside it. Brigid held Máire. Tomás lay with his head against Brigid’s shoulder.

I sealed the lid.

No sickness would enter.

Nothing dead would leave.

---

I am the last now.

The village is silent, but the graves are not.

The doors of the empty houses stand open. Footprints cross the frost from the common field and end beneath my window. Tonight, every buried soul of Kilcrowe has gathered outside the chapel.

They do not scratch.

They wait.

The mare has escaped her paddock. I hear her hooves upon the chapel stones, though the door is barred. The message case hangs from her saddle once more. There is fresh parchment within it.

I know this without seeing.

Something has begun to knock from inside the little coffin.

Three knocks.

A pause.

Then three again.

Brigid always knocked so when she came to my workshop, for she knew I disliked being startled while I worked.

I have set oil around the chancel and piled the parish records upon it. Fire is the only burial left to me.

If this account is found, then the flames failed.

Do not open the lead coffin.

Do not dig beneath the yews.

And if a grey mare is seen upon the road to Kilcrowe, carrying no rider, kill it from afar.

Do not read the message.

It already knows your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**A Leaf Found Blackened at the Edge, the Year Unmarked**

In Fianaise Bhréagach, where the bog drank rain and gave back mist, there came a grief without a name. No bell foretold it. No star marred the whey-white sky. Only the dogs, those lean interpreters, began to whine at empty doors.

First was a heat in the blood, a flood under the skin; then a bruising of the tongue, as though each sinner had swallowed his own confession. Men woke choking, women spoke croaking, and children stared at corners where no saint stood. At noon the lanes lay mute, though behind every shutter came the soft cough, the cut-off laugh, the prayer worn bare by saying.

Father Eoghan wrote *mercy* upon slips of vellum and nailed them above the lintels. By dawn the word had sweated through.

The well tasted of iron. The milk curdled blue. Hens laid eggs with no yolk, only a little coil of hair. We burned juniper, burned linen, burned the beds of the dead; yet the smoke stooped low, a black cloak, and entered every house before us.

Some named the sickness Judgment. Some named it Hunger. Old Máire, whose eyes were filmed but far-seeing, called it the Guest, the Pest, and bade none ask what road it travelled. Nevertheless we barred the western bridge. Nevertheless wet footprints appeared each morning upon the chapel floor, leading inward, never out.

The clerk ceased counting after three score and nine. The priest ceased praying after his teeth loosened in the Host. The bell-rope moved of itself, slow below, though no hand held it; and all night the bronze tongue tolled without sound.

Then the snow came red at the edges.

I write this beneath the table, by tallow shallow and failing. Something in the chimney repeats my name, the same name, softly and wrongly. My wife lies still upstairs. My sons lie beside her, though neither remembers climbing the stair.

In the churchyard, where the yews bend near as eavesdroppers, Donnchadh the undertaker labours alone. He measures no plots now, keeps no lots now, but turns the clotted earth until his palms divide. Before dawn he has opened six graves: three for his children, one for his wife, and two for the neighbors who helped him dig yesterday.

counterfactuals.output:
### Dr. Niamh Kelleher, *The Missing Parishes of Connacht* (2021)

The village of **Dún Caorach** appears on no surviving civil map, parish roll, or census return. Yet its foundations remain in a narrow valley west of Lough Mask: forty-one cottages, a roofless chapel, and a graveyard containing ninety-three unmarked stones.

Indirect evidence places its destruction in the winter of 1843, before the Great Famine. Road ledgers show payments for lime and timber delivered to an unnamed settlement. A magistrate’s diary mentions “the valley quarantine,” though the relevant pages were later cut out. In the spring, Dún Caorach’s baptismal register was burned, its boundary stones overturned, and even its name scraped from diocesan records. No death certificates were issued because, officially, no such village had existed.

The sole account is attributed to **Eamon Rusk**, the village undertaker. His testimony was found in 1978, sewn inside the leather lining of a coffin-maker’s measuring book. The final pages are stained with lime and something long dried to black.

---

> They closed the north road first.
>
> Four constables came with red cloth tied over their mouths and drove stakes into the mud. They stretched chains between them and hung a board:
>
> **BY ORDER OF THE CROWN — NONE SHALL PASS.**
>
> We asked what sickness had warranted it. They would not say. We asked for a physician. They said one was coming. We asked for food.
>
> They backed away from us.
>
> By sunset the south path was blocked as well.
>
> The illness began in the Murphy house. Their youngest girl, Bríd, complained that the chapel bell was ringing beneath her bed. There was no bell in Dún Caorach; Father Devlin had sold it years before. Still, the child heard it. By morning her fever had turned her skin grey about the lips, and every vein in her hands stood dark as writing.
>
> She died before noon.
>
> When I washed her, I found black marks on the soles of her feet, as though she had walked through ashes.
>
> Her mother sickened that night. Then her brothers. Then the neighbours who had helped lay Bríd out.
>
> The physician arrived on the fourth day but would not cross the chain. He shouted questions from horseback while rain filled the road between us. Did the dead cough blood? Some did. Did they bear swellings? No. Did they rave? Yes, but always of the same thing.
>
> A bell under the earth.
>
> He left us two barrels of vinegar, six sacks of lime, and instructions to burn all bedding. He promised broth and medicine on the morrow.
>
> We never saw him again.
>
> At first I made coffins properly. Oak for those who had kept it seasoned, pine for the rest. I planed the boards, pegged the corners, and carved a little cross where the head would lie. By the second week I abandoned the crosses. By the third I abandoned the lids.
>
> There were too many.
>
> Father Devlin went from house to house until the fever took him. He stood in the chapel yard, shaking so violently that his teeth broke, and begged me not to bury him within hearing of the others.
>
> “They are not quiet below,” he said.
>
> I told him it was the fever speaking.
>
> He gripped my coat and answered, “No, Eamon. It is the fever listening.”
>
> He died with blood coming from both ears.
>
> We tried to leave on the eighth day. Twenty-seven of us walked to the northern barrier carrying the children and what food remained. The constables were gone. In their place stood soldiers upon the ridge.
>
> They fired once above our heads.
>
> On the second warning they fired lower.
>
> Old Tomás Bane fell with his cheek torn away. His daughter dragged him back by the ankles while the soldiers shouted that the valley was condemned. That was the word they used—not infected.
>
> **Condemned.**
>
> After that, hunger worked beside the sickness.
>
> Dogs vanished from the lanes. Doors remained open because no one had strength to close them. Each morning I walked with my cart and called out. If a house answered, I passed it. If it did not, I entered.
>
> Sometimes the dead were laid neatly upon beds, coins pressed to their eyelids. Sometimes I found whole families at the door, their fingers worn bloody from clawing at the wood after they had barred themselves in.
>
> They all had ash upon their feet.
>
> Even the infants.
>
> By Candlemas only eleven of us remained alive. We gathered in the chapel, though the roof leaked and the altar had been broken for firewood. Beneath the flagstones came a faint iron tolling.
>
> Once.
>
> Then again.
>
> No one spoke of it. We had grown tired of fear.
>
> Máire Sloane began to laugh. She laughed until her breath stopped, and when we laid her down, the bell beneath us rang a third time.
>
> That night the soldiers brought oil.
>
> We watched their torches moving along the ridge. They burned the cottages at the edge of the village, whether the people inside were dead or not. Smoke rolled downhill and settled over us like a second roof.
>
> I understood then that no rescue had ever been intended. The quarantine was not meant to keep the sickness out of Ireland.
>
> It was meant to keep knowledge of it in Dún Caorach.
>
> I write this in the dead-house beside the graveyard. There are ninety-two stones outside. I have cut the ninety-third for myself.
>
> The others are gone now. I heard the last of them die before dawn. Yet footsteps continue along the road, and hands have begun knocking at the door—not from without, but from beneath the floor.
>
> I have hidden this account where fire may spare it.
>
> If you are reading, do not search old maps for our village. Do not restore our names. Do not ring bells in the valley.
>
> They erased Dún Caorach because every soul here died.
>
> But that is not the same as saying we are dead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gothic folk-horror ballad in paragraph form about a plague-sealed coastal village in 1607. Mention a blood-hoofed horse carrying the closure notice, sentries, the butcher’s shop, mill and church, burning the horse, and a father’s horrifying final act.
counterfactuals.output:
In sixteen hundred and seven, when the black gulls fled the foam, a blood-hoofed horse came over the cliff-road with no rider to guide it home. From its bridle hung the closure notice, stamped with crown and cross: **Let none depart this village, on pain of mortal loss.** The sentries raised their pikes at dawn and barred both strand and brae, while the tide tolled bones beneath the caves and the red sun sickened away.

The butcher’s shop stood shuttered, though the cleaver knocked within; the mill turned on with empty sails, grinding dust as pale as sin. In the church the bell-rope twitched, but no living hand was there, and the saints wore veils of mildew above the plague-dead’s prayer. “Keep your doors and mark your dead, let no soul cross the line”—so cried the sentries through their cloths, in the bitter year of nine-and-seven.

They dragged the blood-hoofed horse to the green and built a pyre of thorn, for some swore plague rode in its mane and death beneath its horn. It screamed like a woman as it burned; the sea drew back in dread, and sparks flew up to the churchyard where the graves would not keep dead. By morning all the village heard hooves pacing under stone, though the horse was ash, the road was watched, and every house alone.

Last was old Tomas, the fisherman, with three small mouths to save; he begged the guards to loose one boat, but they beat him from the wave. At dusk he dressed his children in their Sunday linen white, kissed each brow, and carried them sleeping to the mill beneath the night. He bound them to the turning arms, then cut the brake away, and the great sails woke without a wind before the break of day. Round went his sons and round his girl, above the grinding floor, while Tomas fed himself between the stones—and was a man no more.

Now when plague-mist seals the headland and no star stands on the foam, a blood-hoofed horse bears the closure notice down the road that leads not home. The sentries hear the butcher chop, the empty mill-wheel moan, and from the church three children sing in voices made of stone: “Bar the strand and burn the beast, let neither flesh nor spirit leaven—for the sea keeps all it gathered in sixteen hundred and seven.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce the opening of a found-document horror story: in 2007, an account is uncovered beneath a tree in the square of a razed, quarantined village. The document should sound poetic and archaic while describing how the epidemic consumed everyone and forced the local undertaker to bury his own children.
counterfactuals.output:
### ARCHIVE ITEM 7C  
**Recovered 18 October 2007 from beneath the roots of the ash tree in the former market square of Bellwether, Northumberland.**

The village of Bellwether was placed under military quarantine in February 1911 and razed the following spring. No official census of the dead survives. Recovery personnel found the document sealed in a blackened copper box, together with three children’s milk teeth and a ring of iron keys.

The following is transcribed without correction.

---

I write because there remain none to hear me speak.

The pest came first upon a Thursday, in rain so soft the gutters scarcely murmured. By noon Widow Crake had shut her curtains. By vesper-time the schoolmaster’s little bell was ringing though no hand was seen upon the rope, and the dogs had begun to dig at the churchyard gate.

We called it fever, for men are comforted by the naming of a thing.

Yet fever doth not leave black blossoms beneath the tongue, nor cause the sick to whisper in voices belonging to their dead. Fever doth not pass beneath a bolted door. It doth not know the names of children.

Within seven days every house had tied a rag upon its latch. White for sickness. Black for death. Before the fortnight was ended there was no white cloth left in Bellwether.

I was then sexton, carpenter of coffins, and tender of the graves; and thus did all men come at last unto my keeping. I buried the baker with flour yet beneath his nails. I buried Parson Vale without prayer, for his lips continued moving after his breath had ceased. I buried the constable, the midwife, the drunkard Abel Horn, and all six of the choirboys together, because the earth was frozen and my strength was failing.

Thereafter I ceased the ringing of the bell. Its voice had grown too merry.

My wife, Agnes, was taken on the seventeenth day.

My sons followed her before dawn.

God forgive me, I measured them myself.

Thomas required four feet of pine. Little Edwin wanted scarce three. I planed the boards by candlelight while they lay abed in the next room, and oft I heard one of them turn beneath the sheet, though both were cold and their jaws bound shut.

At sunrise I bore them to the churchyard upon my barrow.

The graves were full.

And from beneath the ground, my children called me Father.
